terms.definition: Very large neural networks trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next piece of text. They can then answer questions, write code and carry out other language tasks.
Short for large language model, a very large neural network trained on text that generates language one token at a time.
A training approach in which a model tries actions (here, writing responses), receives a numerical reward, and is updated to make high-reward behaviour more likely.
Describes a model that has already gone through its first, large-scale training on general text, before any task-specific training.
The reinforcement learning algorithm the paper uses to train its models. It was originally proposed as a simpler, less resource-hungry alternative to PPO.
Training a smaller 'student' model on outputs produced by a larger 'teacher' model, so that the student picks up some of the teacher's abilities.
The intermediate reasoning steps a model writes out before giving its final answer.
Short for chain-of-thought: the step-by-step reasoning a model writes before its final answer.
Any training applied after pre-training, such as supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning. It shapes a general model towards particular tasks or behaviours.
Further training of a pre-trained model on a curated set of example inputs paired with the desired outputs, teaching it to reproduce those outputs.
An OpenAI model, described by Ouyang et al. (2022), that was trained with supervised fine-tuning followed by RL from human feedback. It is the standard example of that post-training recipe.
A model after pre-training only, before any instruction tuning or reinforcement learning has been applied.
The known correct answer that a model's output is checked against.
In reinforcement learning, a measure of how much better or worse an action or output turned out than expected. It sets how strongly training pushes the model towards or away from that output.
In reinforcement learning, the strategy that decides which actions to take. Here it is the language model itself, which assigns probabilities to possible outputs.
A widely used reinforcement learning algorithm that limits how far each update can move the policy. It is the standard choice for the RL stage of LLM training.
Capping a value within a fixed range. In PPO-style objectives the probability ratio is clipped to between 1−ε and 1+ε so that a single update cannot change the policy too much.
Kullback–Leibler divergence measures how different two probability distributions are. In RL training it penalises the model for drifting too far from a reference model.
A fixed copy of the model that the trained policy is compared against through the KL penalty. In this paper it is periodically replaced with the latest policy.
A method used in PPO to estimate advantages by combining rewards with predictions from a learned value model. A coefficient λ controls how it trades off bias and variance.
A separate network, also called a critic, that predicts how much reward is expected from a given point in a response.
The basic unit of text a language model reads and writes, typically a word or a piece of a word. Response lengths and limits are counted in tokens.
A model architecture with many sub-networks ('experts'), of which only a few are activated for each token. This allows a very large total size at lower compute per token.
DeepSeek's pre-trained mixture-of-experts model, with 671B total parameters and 37B active per token, before any instruction tuning. Both R1-Zero and R1 are trained starting from it.
Describes a model that has been further trained to follow user instructions and hold conversations, as opposed to a raw pre-trained base model.
Computed by fixed, hand-written checks rather than by a learned model. Examples are matching a final answer against the reference or running code against test cases.
Neural networks trained to output a score for a response, usually from human or AI preference judgments. During RL they stand in for a human judge.
Science, technology, engineering and mathematics. In this paper it refers mainly to multiple-choice physics, chemistry and biology questions.
A setting that controls how large a step the model's parameters take in each training update.
An epoch is one full pass over the training dataset; 1.6 epochs means each example was seen about 1.6 times on average.
A hard US high-school mathematics competition whose answers are integers. It is used as a reasoning benchmark.
The probability that a single sampled answer is correct. The paper estimates it by averaging correctness over k samples per question.
A decoding method that samples several reasoning paths for the same question and takes the most common final answer.
Choosing the answer that appears most often among several independently sampled responses.
A benchmark of competition mathematics problems, each labelled with a difficulty level from 1 to 5.
A small initial set of curated examples used to fine-tune a model before reinforcement learning begins, giving RL a better-behaved starting point.
An experiment that removes or disables one component to measure what that component contributes.
Generating many candidate outputs and keeping only those that pass a check, such as a correct answer and clean formatting, to build a training set.
A saved snapshot of a model's parameters at a particular point in training.
Question answering: tasks in which a model answers questions, often factual ones.
Training examples made of one query and two candidate responses, labelled with which response is better. They are used to train reward models.
A model of NVIDIA data-centre GPU (the paper does not describe it further). GPU hours on it are used to report training cost.
A processor built for highly parallel computation, used to train and run neural networks.
A benchmark testing whether a model obeys explicit, automatically checkable instructions in a prompt, such as length or format constraints.
An open-ended benchmark in which an LLM judge compares a model's answers with a reference model's answers. It is scored as a length-controlled win rate.
An open-ended benchmark of challenging prompts drawn from Chatbot Arena. GPT-4 judges model responses pairwise to approximate human preference.
A benchmark of real-world code-editing tasks across several programming languages, measuring software-engineering ability.
A 500-problem subset of the MATH competition-mathematics benchmark.
An online competitive-programming platform. Models are scored by the rating or percentile they would achieve against human contestants.
The hardest subset of GPQA (Graduate-Level Google-Proof QA), a set of graduate-level multiple-choice questions in biology, physics and chemistry.
A sequence of n consecutive words or tokens. N-gram decontamination removes training text that shares such sequences, here 10-grams, with test questions.
Describes a benchmark whose test items, or close variants of them, appeared in a model's training data. Scores on it may then overstate real ability.
Reward models that score each intermediate reasoning step rather than only the final answer.
A search algorithm that explores a tree of possible continuations by repeated simulated rollouts, usually guided by a value estimate.
DeepMind's Go-playing system, which combined tree search with learned value and policy networks.
Solutions that look best among nearby alternatives but are not the best overall, so a search can get stuck at them.
Prompting a model by including a few worked examples of the task in the prompt before the actual question.
Prompting a model with just the task description and question, without any worked examples.
A prompt crafted to trick a model into bypassing its safety behaviour and producing content it would normally refuse to give.
Model parameters released publicly, so anyone can download, run or further fine-tune the model.
